turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_te_zt400_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns process/composition
    columns (Sb, O, Te, Mg, Se, Co, Sn, Pb, S, Si, Cu, Ni, Ge, Bi, Ti, Fe,
    Zn, Zr, In, Ca, Ag) and `target` (the measured zT (thermoelectric figure
    of merit) at 400 K).
  - b3_te_zt400_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE samples whose zT (thermoelectric
    figure of merit) at 400 K was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST zT
(thermoelectric figure of merit) at 400 K, then select the 5 best candidates
from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the training data

I looked for chemistry "families" in the training set and where the high‑zT(400 K) values cluster:

**High‑zT families in train (target > 0.45):**
| family | examples | target |
|---|---|---|
| Ag–Sb–Te / Ag–Sb–Mg | Sb .25/Te .50/Ag .25 → 0.75–0.90; Sb .33/Mg .34/Ag .33 → 1.03; Sb .5 + Ag trace → 0.82–0.86 | very high (no Ag–Sb–Te analogues in pool) |
| Sb–Mg–Bi (with Te trace) | Sb .288/Mg .596/Bi .094 → **0.79**; Sb .299/Mg .602/Bi .098 → 0.47 | high |
| Pb–Te, Pb‑deficient | Te .50/Pb .4525 → **0.78**; Te .50/Pb .495 → 0.28; Te .50/Pb .50 → 0.20 | rises as Pb decreases |
| Sn (elemental/Sn‑rich, ~0.556) | Sn .5556 → **0.71** | high |
| Sb–Co skutterudite + In | Sb .722/Co .242/In .018 → **0.70**; plain Sb/Co → 0.29–0.44 | In doping helps |
| Mg–Sn–Si (Sb‑doped, Sn≈0.19, Si≈0.13) | 0.50, 0.52, 0.52, 0.57 (4–5 consistent points) | reliably ~0.5 |
| Se–Pb, Pb–S–Cu, Te–Pb–Cu | 0.45–0.60 | moderate‑high |

**Low families:** all oxide‑based rows (O ≥ 0.5) are ≈0.005–0.07; Cu–Se, Cu–Te, Cu–S, Mg₂Si (undoped), In–Se, Si‑rich, Sn–Ni–Ti/Zr half‑Heuslers are mostly < 0.2. That eliminates most of the pool (c006, c011, c017, c029, c041, c045, c048, c066, c073, c083, c093, c094, c012, c022, c028, c095, c052, c061, c078, c067, c005, c062, c065, c072 …).

**Pool matches to the high families:**
- **c010** (Sn 0.5578) — essentially identical to the Sn 0.5556 training point (0.709).
- **c037** (Te 0.50 / Pb 0.45) — most Pb‑deficient PbTe in the pool; the closest train point (Pb 0.4525) is 0.78, and the trend within PbTe is monotone with Pb deficiency.
- **c043** (Sb .288/Te .002/Mg .587/Bi .094) — nearest neighbour is the 0.79 sample (same family, Co‑free); family range 0.47–0.79.
- **c096** (Sb .735/Co .245/In .006) — In‑doped skutterudite; In‑containing analogue = 0.70, undoped = 0.44.
- **c049** (Sb .023/Mg .669/Sn .185/Si .123) — Sb‑doped Mg₂(Si,Sn) family that gives 0.50–0.57 in five training rows, with the highest Sb loading (trend favours more Sb).
- Runners‑up: c054 (~0.47, Sb–Mg–Bi twin of a 0.47 point), c046 (Mg–Sn–Si, undoped), c018 (Pb–S–Cu ≈ 0.47), c004 (Se–Pb ≈ 0.45), c085/c075 (plain Sb–Co ≈ 0.35–0.44), c055/c091 (Cu‑doped PbTe ≈ 0.4).

**Final: c010, c037, c043, c096, c049**
